title: No idols
hook: don't make God small enough to carry

segments.voice: Yesterday, no other gods: nothing else in first place. Your line was first things first. What got your first five minutes? Day one thousand one hundred eighty-five.

A procession is moving, and the gods are riding on pack animals. In Isaiah, the images of Bel and Nebo are loaded onto beasts and cattle: "your carriages were heavy loaden; they are a burden to the weary beast." Then he describes what people do with a god they've made. "They bear him upon the shoulder, they carry him, and set him in his place, and he standeth; from his place shall he not remove." A god you have to haul around. A god that stays exactly where you put it. Today: no idols, and the risk of making God small enough to carry.

The commandment says it plainly: "Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image." Orthodox and Reformed Christians count it as a word of its own; Catholics and Lutherans read it as part of the first. Either way, the worry is the same. An idol is a god cut down to size. You made it, so it can't surprise you. You set it down, so it stays put. And Isaiah turns the picture over. A few verses earlier, God speaks: "even to hoar hairs will I carry you: I have made, and I will bear; even I will carry, and will deliver you." Idols are carried. God carries. Churches have drawn the line on images in different places. Orthodox Christians fill their churches with icons and venerate them, and they draw a firm line between honoring an image and worshipping it. Catholics use statues and paintings and teach, as the Orthodox do, that the honor passes to the one shown. Reformed churches have tended to keep worship plain, wary of images in worship at all. Each is taking the same warning seriously. But the commandment reaches past wood and paint. A god can be carved out of ideas, too: a God who shares all your opinions, who likes exactly the people you like, who never asks for anything inconvenient. That god fits in a pocket. The God of Isaiah doesn't. A little further on he asks, "To whom will ye liken me?" And a few verses later the answer comes: "I am God, and there is none like me."
screen: `A GOD THAT FITS IN A POCKET.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice where you've shrunk God. Settle, and breathe. Ask quietly: where does God always seem to agree with me? Which people do I picture God not bothering with? What would I never expect God to ask? Let one small picture come up, the pocket-sized one. Don't fight it. Just notice its edges. Then set Isaiah's question beside it: to whom will ye liken me? If you pray, you can sit with that question before God, without rushing to answer. The bell holds the time.
No idols. Not making God small enough to carry, in wood or stone, or in the ideas we keep in our pockets.
Your line: god is bigger. Today, when you catch yourself sure of exactly what God thinks of someone, stop, and leave some room. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-five.

howItsDone: Christians apply this commandment differently: Orthodox churches are filled with icons that believers venerate, Catholic churches use statues and paintings, and Reformed churches tend to keep worship spaces plain; preachers in each often extend it to the ideas people make of God.

fork.setup: you're Isaiah, watching the images of Bel and Nebo sway past on tired animals. what do you point out?
options: how beautifully the images are made.
that these gods have to be carried, while God carries his people.
that the procession is far too long.
fork.reveal: the idols are "a burden to the weary beast." God says instead: "I have made, and I will bear; even I will carry."

original.note: Hebrew: a carved image. The graven image of Exodus 20:4.

trapdoor: what you thought: no idols is about not keeping statues.
what it means: don't shrink God into something you made, can carry and can control, in stone or in ideas.
what a scholar hears: in Isaiah 46 the images of Bel and Nebo are loaded on animals, while God says, I will carry you.

Editor pass: hook said the gods ride 'in carts'; in the KJV 'carriages' means the loads carried, and Isaiah 46:1 puts the idols on beasts and cattle, so the hook and screen now say pack animals. Teach's 'the question is left hanging, on purpose' was wrong (Isaiah 46:9 answers it); now quotes 46:9 and cites it.
